title: 1099-NEC vs W-2: who gets which form
description: Decision table for common-law employees (W-2) versus independent contractors paid $600+ (1099-NEC), compiled from IRS contractor/employee guidance. Not tax or employment-law advice.
extract: The form follows the relationship, not the worker’s preference. A common-law employee is reported on Form W-2. The IRS looks at behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship (written contract, benefits, permanence, whether the work is a key business activity). An independent contractor paid $600 or more of nonemployee compensation in the year is generally reported on Form 1099-NEC. Payments under that $600 federal 1099-NEC threshold do not require a 1099-NEC, though records still matter. The same person can be a W-2 employee for one role and a 1099-NEC contractor for a separate, genuinely independent engagement. Form 1099-K (payment cards and third-party networks) is a different form and is not a substitute for W-2 or 1099-NEC. This page is a decision table, not a facts-and-circumstances opinion. Compiled 2026-08-29 from IRS independent-contractor guidance and Form 1099-NEC instructions. Not tax or employment-law advice.

faq.q: Does calling someone a contractor avoid a W-2?
faq.a: No. If the payer has the right to control how the work is done, the IRS treats the worker as an employee regardless of the contract label.
Generally when you pay an unincorporated independent contractor $600 or more of nonemployee compensation in the year.
No. 1099-K reports certain payment-card and third-party network transactions. Employee wages still go on a W-2.
